content: Collective consciousness refers to the shared beliefs and moral attitudes that function as a unifying force within a society. This concept was introduced by the French sociologist Émile Durkheim (1858–1917) in his works, including The Division of Labour (1893), The Rules of Sociological Method (1895), Suicide (1897), and The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912). In The Division of Labour, Durkheim argued that in traditional or simpler societies—those organized around clan, family, or tribal relationships—religion played a central role in uniting members by fostering a shared consciousness, referred to in French as conscience collective. In such societies, the individual’s consciousness is largely aligned with that of the collective, creating what Durkheim termed mechanical solidarity, which is based on mutual similarity among members. As societies evolve and become more individualistic, the structure of the division of labor replaces this mechanical solidarity with organic solidarity. This new form of solidarity arises from the interdependence of individuals performing specialized roles, reducing the reliance on collective consciousness. However, as the collective consciousness diminishes, individuals may become vulnerable to anomie, a state characterized by a lack of shared values and an increasing sense of purposelessness. The term collective consciousness has also been used in other contexts. For example, in Sahaja Yoga, it is described as an outcome of meditation and self-realization. Additionally, modern sociologists have identified various manifestations of collective consciousness in contemporary societies, ranging from solidarity attitudes and shared cultural memes to extreme phenomena such as groupthink or herd behavior. This concept has been developed to explain how entire communities come together to adopt and share similar values.
